```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(ranger)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
set.seed(605)
```

## Why this matters

Marine survey effort is not a random sample of the ocean. It follows ports, weather windows,
vessel availability, funding cycles and the last decade's research priorities. Shallow water near
a lab is sampled hundreds of times; the shelf break in February is sampled never.

A model built on that effort learns the relationships that hold *where you went*. Ask it about
anywhere else and it will answer — confidently, with no warning — and this page measures how wrong
that answer is, using the simulation's known truth to do it.

There are two distinct problems here and they need separating. **Uneven sampling** means some
regions of the environment are represented weakly. **Extrapolation** means some are not
represented at all. The second is the one that ends careers, and the trap is that it is hard to
detect: a station can be inside the observed range of every single variable and still be somewhere
your survey has never been.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

### What each model family does past the edge

Nothing in a fitted model marks where the data stopped. Asked about a station outside it, each
family does something different and none of them says so.

| Family | Beyond the data | Failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear regression | Continues the straight line forever | Impossible values, eventually |
| Polynomial | Follows the curve's own logic | Violent; the curve was never meant to go there |
| GAM | Extends the spline, with rapidly widening intervals | At least the intervals warn you |
| **Trees, forests, boosting** | **Repeats the nearest leaf's value** | Flat, plausible-looking, and silently wrong |
| Neural network | Whatever the activations do out there | Unpredictable |

The tree row is the dangerous one, and it runs against intuition. A forest never produces an
absurd number, which makes it feel safe outside the data. What it actually does is repeat the
value from the closest region it *did* see — so if abundance was falling with depth when the data
ran out, the forest predicts that it simply stops falling.

## Worked example

We simulate a common situation: a survey that only worked shallow water, and a model asked to map
the deeper shelf.

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  inner_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id")

d <- survey |>
  select(station_id, true_mean, abundance, depth_m, temperature_c,
         chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()

shallow <- filter(d, depth_m < 100)
deep    <- filter(d, depth_m >= 100)

c(`training stations (< 100 m)` = nrow(shallow),
  `stations to predict (>= 100 m)` = nrow(deep),
  `deepest training station` = max(shallow$depth_m),
  `deepest station overall` = max(deep$depth_m)) |>
  round(1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fit
parametric <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2, raw = TRUE) +
  poly(temperature_c, 2, raw = TRUE) + log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + substrate
all_vars <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

predictions <- function(train, newdata) {
  list(
    `Linear (quadratic terms)` = predict(lm(parametric, data = train), newdata),
    `Poisson GLM`  = predict(glm(parametric, data = train, family = poisson),
                             newdata, type = "response"),
    `Random forest` = predict(ranger(all_vars, data = train, num.trees = 400, seed = 1),
                              newdata)$predictions
  )
}

extrapolated <- predictions(shallow, deep)
```

Because the survey is simulated we can compare against `true_mean`, the expected count the
generating process used — so the comparison is not blurred by negative-binomial noise.

```{r}
#| label: bias
set.seed(3)
inner <- sample(nrow(shallow), round(0.75 * nrow(shallow)))
in_range <- predictions(shallow[inner, ], shallow[-inner, ])

tibble(
  model = names(extrapolated),
  `in-range bias` = map_dbl(in_range, \(p) mean(p) / mean(shallow$true_mean[-inner]) - 1),
  `extrapolated bias` = map_dbl(extrapolated, \(p) mean(p) / mean(deep$true_mean) - 1)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(100 * x, 1))) |>
  rename(`in-range bias %` = `in-range bias`,
         `extrapolated bias %` = `extrapolated bias`)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-extrapolation
#| fig-cap: "Mean prediction against the true mean, in depth bands. Left of the dashed line is where the models were trained; right of it they are extrapolating. Beyond the boundary the truth keeps falling — from 3.7 to 1.1 individuals — while the random forest flattens near 5, the Poisson GLM flattens near 3.5, and the quadratic turns back upward, finishing highest of the three."
#| fig-alt: "A line chart with depth band on the horizontal axis running from zero-to-40 metres through to 160-to-200 metres, and mean count from about 1 to 7 on the vertical. A dashed vertical line after the 70-to-100 band separates training from extrapolation. A thick black truth line starts at 7.2, drops steeply to 4.4, eases to 3.9 and 3.7 at the boundary, then continues down through 3.3 and 2.1 to 1.1 in the deepest band. In the shallowest band all three model lines sit about a unit below the truth; through the middle training bands they track it closely. To the right of the dashed line the random forest line jumps to 5.3, stays there for two bands and ends near 4.9; the Poisson line sits flat between 3.5 and 3.7; and the linear line climbs steadily from 3.7 to 5.1, ending above the random forest and nearly five units above the truth."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
band_edges <- c(0, 40, 70, 100, 120, 140, 160, 200)

both <- bind_rows(
  shallow |> mutate(!!!predictions(shallow, shallow)),
  deep    |> mutate(!!!extrapolated)
) |>
  mutate(band = cut(depth_m, band_edges, include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  summarise(
    across(c(Truth = true_mean, `Linear (quadratic terms)`,
             `Poisson GLM`, `Random forest`), mean),
    .by = band
  ) |>
  arrange(band) |>
  pivot_longer(-band, names_to = "series", values_to = "mean_count")

ggplot(both, aes(band, mean_count, colour = series, group = series,
                 linewidth = series == "Truth")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.4, `FALSE` = 0.8), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    Truth = "grey15",
    `Linear (quadratic terms)` = ml_palette[["blue"]],
    `Poisson GLM` = ml_palette[["green"]],
    `Random forest` = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]
  )) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 6.6, label = "trained here", size = 3.4,
           colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 6.6, label = "extrapolating", size = 3.4,
           colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  labs(x = "Depth band (m)", y = "Mean count", colour = NULL,
       title = "What happens when the data runs out")
```

### The harder problem: novel combinations

The example above is easy to spot — you can see that you are predicting at 180 m having trained
below 100 m. The dangerous case is subtler. Suppose the survey only sailed in summer and autumn,
and the model is asked about spring and winter.

```{r}
#| label: novelty
environment_only <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu")

sampled   <- d |> filter(season %in% c("summer", "autumn")) |> select(all_of(environment_only))
unsampled <- d |> filter(season %in% c("spring", "winter")) |> select(all_of(environment_only))

# Check 1: is each variable inside the range the survey saw?
within_range <- map_dfc(environment_only, \(v) {
  tibble(!!v := unsampled[[v]] >= min(sampled[[v]]) & unsampled[[v]] <= max(sampled[[v]]))
})
univariate_ok <- rowSums(within_range) == length(environment_only)

# Check 2: is the *combination* one the survey saw?
centre <- colMeans(sampled)
spread <- cov(sampled)
threshold <- quantile(mahalanobis(sampled, centre, spread), 0.95)
jointly_novel <- mahalanobis(unsampled, centre, spread) > threshold

tibble(
  `stations to predict` = nrow(unsampled),
  `inside every variable's range` = sum(univariate_ok),
  `outside the joint 95% region` = sum(jointly_novel),
  `passes every single-variable check but is jointly novel` = sum(univariate_ok & jointly_novel)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-novelty
#| fig-cap: "Temperature against chlorophyll, for a survey that sailed only in summer and autumn (grey) and the spring and winter stations it is being asked about. Orange stations are inside the surveyed range of every variable taken one at a time, yet sit in a combination of conditions the survey essentially never encountered — cold water with high chlorophyll, which is a spring bloom."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter plot with temperature from 2 to 16 degrees on the horizontal axis and chlorophyll on a logarithmic vertical axis from 0.07 to 14. Grey points, the summer and autumn survey, form a broad cloud concentrated between 8 and 16 degrees with chlorophyll mostly under 3. Blue points sit within that cloud. Orange points cluster to the upper left of it — colder than 9 degrees and with chlorophyll above 2 — a region where grey points are sparse. A dashed rectangle marks the surveyed range of each variable separately, and almost all the orange points fall inside it."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
novelty_plot <- unsampled |>
  mutate(status = case_when(
    univariate_ok & jointly_novel ~ "Passes every single-variable check, but novel",
    jointly_novel                 ~ "Outside a variable's range",
    TRUE                          ~ "Genuinely covered"
  ))

ggplot(mapping = aes(temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3)) +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = min(sampled$temperature_c), xmax = max(sampled$temperature_c),
           ymin = min(sampled$chlorophyll_mg_m3), ymax = max(sampled$chlorophyll_mg_m3),
           fill = NA, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = sampled, colour = "grey75", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = novelty_plot, aes(colour = status), size = 1.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    `Passes every single-variable check, but novel` = ml_palette[["orange"]],
    `Outside a variable's range` = ml_palette[["blue"]],
    `Genuinely covered` = ml_palette[["sky"]]
  )) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Chlorophyll (mg m⁻³, log scale)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Inside every range, outside the survey",
       subtitle = "Grey: the summer/autumn survey. Dashed box: each variable's observed range.")
```

## What the results mean

**In range, all three models are honest on average.** Predicting held-out shallow stations, the
biases are +2%, +5% and +8%. They do under-predict the very shallowest band, where the truth is
7.2 and all three say about 6 — the smoothing you would expect at the edge of any dataset — but
nothing here is broken.

**Past the edge, they diverge sharply and none of them warns you.**

| Model | Bias in range | Bias extrapolating |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson GLM | +5% | **+19%** |
| Linear with quadratics | +2% | **+39%** |
| Random forest | +8% | **+73%** |

The forest is the worst by a wide margin, and the depth-band figure shows exactly why. Between
160 and 200 m the true mean count is **1.05**; the forest predicts **4.91**, nearly five times
too high, and it predicts almost the same value at 100 m as at 190 m. It has no mechanism for
"keeps decreasing". It repeats the last thing it saw.

The Poisson GLM does better because its functional form carries an instruction about what happens
next, and on the log scale that instruction keeps bending downward — though it too flattens out
around 3.5 rather than following the truth to 1.1.

The linear model with quadratic terms shows the other failure in the table. It tracks the decline
for one band past the boundary and then **turns back upward**, finishing at 5.1 in the deepest
band — above the forest, and nearly five times the truth. A quadratic has a turning point; fitted
to shallow data, that turning point lands somewhere arbitrary, and past it the curve rises. This
is the same arithmetic that put [the linearity page's](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) depth
optimum at 293 m, beyond any station in the survey.

**And the range check you would naturally run does not catch the hard case.** Of the 356
spring-and-winter stations, **251 (71%)** are inside the observed range of every single variable.
But **143 of them — 40% of all the stations to be predicted — are simultaneously inside every
individual range and outside the region the survey actually occupied.** Those are cold, high-
chlorophyll stations: a spring bloom. The survey saw cold water (in autumn) and it saw high
chlorophyll (in summer), just never together.

::: {.callout-important}
Checking `min()` and `max()` of each predictor is the standard extrapolation check and it is not
sufficient. Combinations matter, and as the number of predictors grows the surveyed region becomes
a vanishingly small part of the box that contains it. Report a multivariate novelty measure —
Mahalanobis distance to the training centre, distance to the nearest training point, or a formal
tool such as ExDet — alongside any prediction map.
:::

## Where this breaks down

**Mahalanobis distance assumes an ellipse.** It treats the surveyed region as one ellipsoid around
the mean, which is reasonable for roughly symmetric predictors and wrong when the survey covers two
separate clusters — inshore and offshore, say. Then the gap between them scores as covered, when
it is exactly the place with no data. A nearest-neighbour distance handles that shape better.

**Extrapolating is sometimes the whole point.** Climate projections require predicting temperatures
no survey has recorded. The answer is not to refuse, but to be explicit: state that the prediction
is an extrapolation, prefer a model whose functional form you can defend mechanistically over a
flexible one, and widen the uncertainty far beyond what the model reports.

**Uneven sampling biases the fit, not just the coverage.** If 80% of your stations are shallow, the
fitted relationship is mostly a shallow-water relationship, and it will be reported as though it
applied everywhere. Weighting, or stratified resampling, addresses this; noticing it is the harder
part.

**The forest's flatness is not always worse.** Where the true relationship really does saturate —
many physiological responses do — repeating the last value is more nearly right than a quadratic
that keeps bending. The forest's failure here is specific: the truth kept declining. Which
behaviour is safer depends on knowing something about the process, which is a scientific judgement
and not a modelling one.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- Models do not know where their data stopped. They answer anyway, with no warning attached.
- **Trees and forests flatten past the edge**, repeating the nearest leaf. Here the forest
  predicted 4.91 against a true 1.05 in the 160–200 m band.
- Extrapolation bias in this example: Poisson GLM **+19%**, linear-with-quadratics **+39%**,
  random forest **+73%** — from models biased by 2–8% in range.
- A per-variable range check is not enough. **40% of the stations to be predicted passed every
  single-variable check while sitting outside the region the survey occupied.**
- Report a multivariate novelty measure with any prediction map, and say plainly which parts of it
  are extrapolation.

:::

## Try it yourself

1. Refit the forest with `min_n = 50` so its leaves are much larger, and re-check the deep bands.
   Does a smoother forest extrapolate any better, and what does your answer say about whether
   tuning can fix this?
2. Replace the Mahalanobis check with the distance from each unsampled station to its nearest
   sampled station in standardised predictor space. How many stations does that flag which the
   ellipse did not, and where are they?
